questions.question: In a Schnorr sigma protocol transcript (t, c, s), which verifier equation is checked?
options: g^s == t · y^c (mod p)
y^s == t · g^c (mod p)
g^t == s · y^c (mod p)
g^s == y · t^c (mod p)
questions.explanation: Schnorr verification checks that the response s opens the commitment t consistently with statement y = g^x.

questions.question: What is the goal of a knowledge extractor in a proof of knowledge definition?
options: Recover a valid witness if a prover convinces the verifier often enough
Simulate a transcript without interacting with the prover
Find a hash collision to break Fiat–Shamir
Compute the discrete logarithm of every group element
questions.explanation: Knowledge soundness is formalized by the existence of an extractor that outputs a witness when the prover has a non-negligible success probability.

questions.question: Special soundness for a sigma protocol typically says an extractor can compute a witness from:
options: Two accepting transcripts with the same commitment and different challenges
Two rejecting transcripts with different commitments and the same challenge
One accepting transcript and one rejecting transcript for the same challenge
Any single accepting transcript
questions.explanation: The extractor needs a 'collision' on the first message (commitment) and two distinct challenges to eliminate randomness and solve for the witness.

questions.question: Given Schnorr transcripts (t, c, s) and (t, c', s') that both verify and have c ≠ c' (mod q), which formula extracts x (mod q)?
questions.explanation: Subtracting the two response equations cancels the nonce r and leaves x multiplied by (c - c'), which you invert modulo q.

questions.question: Why does the extractor need 'rewinding' access (or an equivalent forking ability) in many PoK proofs?
options: To obtain two different challenges for the same commitment
To learn the prover's random seed directly from memory
To make the verifier accept even when the statement is false
To avoid modular arithmetic entirely
questions.explanation: Special soundness extraction requires two accepting transcripts that share the same first message; rewinding is how the proof obtains them.

questions.question: In an OR proof built from two Schnorr branches, you get two accepting OR transcripts with the same commitments but different global challenges. What can you extract?
options: A witness for at least one branch
Witnesses for both branches
Only the prover's nonce r, never a witness
Nothing; OR proofs are never proofs of knowledge
questions.explanation: Different global challenges force at least one branch to have different per-branch challenges, enabling Schnorr extraction for that branch.

questions.question: Attack scenario: a prover accidentally reuses the same Schnorr nonce r (same commitment t) in two sessions with different challenges c and c'. What is the consequence?
options: The witness x can be recovered from the two transcripts
Nothing changes; reusing r only affects performance
Only the public key y leaks, not x
Verification fails automatically in both sessions
questions.explanation: Nonce reuse gives exactly the two-transcript condition special soundness needs, so x is computed as (s - s') / (c - c') mod q.

questions.question: In Schnorr, which modulus is used for computing the response s = r + c·x?
options: Modulo q (the subgroup order / scalar field)
Modulo p (the group modulus)
Modulo (p - 1) always
No modulus is needed
questions.explanation: The response lives in the scalar field Z_q; group operations like exponentiation happen modulo p.
